quick: Empty stomach: 1 h before or 2 h after food
Excreted in milk; use with caution
Renal, hepatic, hematologic on prolonged use
summary: Ampicillin is a broad-spectrum aminopenicillin effective against many gram-positive and gram-negative organisms, used for genitourinary, GI, respiratory tract infections, gonorrhea and meningococcal disease. It is acid-stable and orally absorbed but should be taken on an empty stomach. Bactericidal via cell-wall synthesis inhibition; the chief risk is hypersensitivity including anaphylaxis.
indications: Genitourinary tract infections including gonorrhea (susceptible organisms)
Gastrointestinal tract infections (Shigella, Salmonella, E. coli, P. mirabilis, enterococci)
Respiratory tract infections (non-penicillinase H. influenzae, staphylococci, streptococci incl. S. pneumoniae)

dosage.d: 500 mg qid in equally spaced doses

dosage.c: Respiratory tract infection, adult & child >20 kg
dosage.d: 250 mg qid in equally spaced doses
3.5 g orally once with 1 g probenecid
dosage.n: Use no less than this dose; obtain follow-up cultures 7-14 days

dosage.d: 100 mg/kg/day, divided qid in equally spaced doses

admin: Take on an empty stomach, at least 30 min before or 2 h after meals for maximal absorption
Take with a full 8 oz glass of water
Continue therapy at least 48-72 h after becoming asymptomatic (except single-dose gonorrhea regimen)
For hemolytic streptococcal infections treat a minimum of 10 days to prevent rheumatic fever/glomerulonephritis
Screen for penicillin/cephalosporin allergy before starting; do not use smaller-than-recommended doses
moa: Ampicillin inhibits bacterial cell-wall biosynthesis by binding penicillin-binding proteins, blocking transpeptidation/cross-linking of peptidoglycan during active multiplication. The resulting defective cell wall produces a bactericidal effect against susceptible gram-positive and many gram-negative organisms. Resistance is mediated chiefly by beta-lactamases that cleave the beta-lactam ring.

absolute: History of serious hypersensitivity (anaphylaxis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome) to ampicillin or other beta-lactams
Prior cholestatic jaundice/hepatic dysfunction associated with ampicillin
relative: History of cephalosporin or multiple-allergen sensitivity
Severe renal impairment without dose adjustment

preg: Animal reproduction studies show no evidence of impaired fertility or fetal harm, but there are no adequate well-controlled studies in pregnant women. Use during pregnancy only if clearly needed.
lact: Ampicillin-class antibiotics are excreted in breast milk and may sensitize the infant. Exercise caution when administering to a nursing woman; monitor infant for diarrhea, rash or candidiasis.
renal: Ampicillin is excreted largely unchanged in urine, so accumulation occurs in renal impairment. Reduce dose or extend the dosing interval according to degree of impairment. Ampicillin-class antibiotics are removed by hemodialysis (but not peritoneal dialysis); supplement after dialysis.
hepatic: Hepatic dysfunction including hepatitis and cholestatic jaundice has been reported and is usually reversible, though deaths have occurred. Monitor hepatic function at regular intervals in patients with hepatic impairment. Contraindicated if there is a prior history of ampicillin-associated cholestatic jaundice/hepatic dysfunction.

major: Allopurinol - substantially increased incidence of skin rash
Probenecid - decreases renal tubular secretion of ampicillin, raising blood levels and toxicity risk
moderate: Oral anticoagulants (warfarin) - possible enhanced anticoagulant effect; monitor INR
Bacteriostatic antibiotics (chloramphenicol, erythromycins, sulfonamides, tetracyclines) - may antagonize the bactericidal effect of penicillins (in vitro)
minor: Oral contraceptives - may be less effective with increased breakthrough bleeding; advise backup contraception
interactions.food: Food impairs absorption; take at least 30 min before or 2 h after meals despite acid stability.
interactions.diagnostics: May cause false-positive urine glucose with copper-reduction (Clinitest) tests; use enzymatic glucose oxidase methods. Periodic renal, hepatic and hematopoietic evaluation advised on prolonged high-dose therapy.

serious: Severe cutaneous reactions (SJS, TEN, DRESS, AGEP, exfoliative dermatitis)
rare: Hepatic dysfunction / cholestatic jaundice, SGOT elevation
Anemia, thrombocytopenia, thrombocytopenic purpura, leukopenia, agranulocytosis, eosinophilia
Linear IgA bullous dermatosis, laryngeal stridor, high fever
emergency: Anaphylaxis (airway swelling, hypotension) - treat with epinephrine

monitoring: Renal, hepatic and hematopoietic function periodically on prolonged or high-dose therapy
Hepatic function at regular intervals in patients with hepatic impairment
Signs of superinfection (Candida, Pseudomonas, C. difficile)
Allergic reactions, especially early after the first dose
Follow-up cultures (gonorrhea at 7-14 days; streptococci after completing treatment)
counsel: Take on an empty stomach with a full glass of water; complete the entire course
Report rash, hives, swelling, mucosal lesions or breathing difficulty immediately
Report watery or bloody diarrhea, which may occur up to 2 months after treatment
Avoid if you have mononucleosis (glandular fever) due to high rash risk
Use additional contraception if on hormonal contraceptives
pk: Bactericidal soon after absorption during active bacterial multiplication
~3.0 mcg/mL serum after a 500 mg oral capsule
Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F); dispense in a tight container
pearls: High rate of maculopapular rash in mononucleosis/EBV - avoid ampicillin in these patients
Acid-stable but food reduces absorption, so dose on an empty stomach (unlike amoxicillin)
Penetrates CSF only when meninges are inflamed - useful in meningitis
Least protein-bound penicillin (~20%); excreted largely unchanged in urine
Allopurinol co-administration markedly increases rash incidence
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as remembered. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and resume the regular schedule; do not double the dose.
overdose: In overdose, discontinue medication and treat symptomatically with supportive measures. GI symptoms and fluid/electrolyte imbalance may occur. In patients with renal impairment, ampicillin-class antibiotics can be removed by hemodialysis but not by peritoneal dialysis.
